title: A website that feels like her chair.
problem: The site had to do more than show good hair. A new client needs to know what to choose, what it may cost, and how to book.
kept: Rachel’s point of view, her work, and the Square setup that was already part of the business.
changed: We brought her work, service details, pricing, and booking into one clear site. The Hair Brief gives unsure visitors a place to start.
result: A new visitor can meet the stylist, see her work, and compare the options before choosing a booking or a conversation.
body: Hair By Rachel Charles is an independent hair studio in Phoenix. Color, cuts, and extensions all start with a conversation. We built a website that brings that care online. Visitors can see the work, compare services, and find a clear next step.

The yellow, bold type, and close views of the work give the site a clear point of view. It does not look like a stock salon page. The portrait puts a person beside the name, while the work shows what the studio is about.
That first impression has a job. A visitor should know whose chair they are considering. Services and prices sit close to the work, so style does not come at the cost of useful facts.
Someone who knows the service can head to booking. Someone who is unsure can use the Hair Brief. It starts with a goal and leaves room for hair history, upkeep, time, and budget.
The brief offers a starting point for a talk. It does not promise a hair result. That leaves the final choice with the client and stylist, where it belongs.
The site keeps Square in the booking path. The current booking page separates service, time, and contact details. Nothing is booked by looking at the page.

Service pages, pricing, and a first-visit guide each have a clear home. Links connect those pages without making someone search through a social feed. The same tasks stay available on a phone, tablet, or desktop.
The result is a useful front door for a one-person business. It shows the work and explains the next step, while keeping the booking tool already in place.

title: The film sets the mood. The website gives it a home.
problem: A film website must work for fans, press, and people in the film business. Each group needs a different piece of the story.
kept: The film’s artwork, dark tone, official credits, and the client’s own film material.
changed: We gave the trailer, press, credits, and photo archive clear places. Contact choices help each type of visitor start the right conversation.
result: Visitors have one official source for the film and a clear path to its trailer, press material, and premiere archive.
body: CC Films is a film company in Dallas. Its website presents Marrow, a psychological horror film. We built a home for the trailer, film details, press links, and premiere photos. The site keeps the film’s tone without making people hunt for the facts.
The film’s poster leads the page. Deep color, tall type, and fine rules keep the mood close to the work. The website does not need to compete with the film or add a second visual story.
Useful labels sit around that mood. A visitor can watch, read, or contact the company without guessing what a symbol means. On a phone, the poster and next steps keep their own space.
A premiere is a night. Its photos can stay useful long after it ends. The gallery gives that material its own page, with event context and photo credit.
A clear archive helps a guest find the event again. It also gives press and collaborators a direct source to share. The photographer’s credit stays with the material.
The trailer has a clear watch link. Press references lead to their sources, while company and film credits remain readable text. The contact form separates the reason for an inquiry.
The gallery is linked from the main site rather than left on a separate, hard-to-find page. The desktop and phone layouts present the same official material at different sizes.
This is not a claim that the website earned press coverage. It is a record of the home we built for the film’s existing work, and the paths that help visitors use it.

title: Show the craft. Make the first step clear.
problem: Painting and murals share craft, but they start with different questions. The website needed to show the difference without splitting the business in two.
kept: The studio’s identity, project work, local focus, and practical way of talking about a job.
changed: We separated painting and mural paths, brought project images forward, and placed the next inquiry beside the relevant work.
result: A visitor can see the type of work that fits their space, learn about the process, and choose the right project conversation.
body: Chromatic Painting & Design paints homes and business spaces. It also makes murals. The studio works in Greater Phoenix, with murals across Arizona. We built a site that shows both sides of the work. Good paint work and original art share one home.

Place and color lead the site. Large photos show the work at its real scale. Warm tones and clear type give the studio room to feel like itself. The page does not look like a stock paint-company site.
Each image has a job. A room, a house, and a large wall need different kinds of care. We use the photos to make those needs easy to see. The work leads. The next step stays close.
The paint pages explain the work around a home or shop. They cover the space, access, prep, and steps of a job. A visitor can learn what to ask before a site visit.
Murals have their own path. It starts with an idea and a wall, not a box meant for a paint quote. The site keeps both kinds of work under one name.
Work examples link to the right service page. That page leads to a call or a project request. The phone layout keeps those choices clear. It does not squeeze a large menu into a small screen.
The site shows job stages and a before-and-after example. Those photos show the studio’s craft. They do not prove that the website caused more sales.
The site gives the studio one clear home. Each kind of work has its own path. A visitor can see what fits their space and ask about a project.

title: A place to start when help is hard to find.
problem: Someone looking for help may have little time or energy. The website needed a clear starting point and plain words for real situations.
kept: The goal of connecting people with resources, and separate paths for finding help and offering it.
changed: We organized the public site around needs and location. Clear labels, large choices, and nearby safety information guide the first steps.
result: People can start with a need or place, then look for a relevant resource. Those offering help have a separate path.
body: ClearHelp helps people look for food, housing, and other local help. It also gives people a way to offer help. We built the public site around what a person needs. They should not have to learn how an agency sorts its work first.
Bright colors separate the main choices. Short questions help a person start. There is room around each button, so the page does not feel crowded. The style is warm, but the task stays clear.
On a phone, search and the main menu each have their own space. We kept the first page focused on the next step. It does not start with a wall of rules or office names.
The needs page uses plain words for real situations. A person can start with food, housing, safety, or another need. They do not have to guess which group might handle it.
A place search offers another way in. The site helps a person find a source to check. It cannot promise that a group has space or can help right away.
Need pages, place search, and ways to give help link together. The key facts stay in readable text. A person does not need a chart to learn where to go.
The quick-exit button has a clear limit beside it. Leaving the page does not erase browser history. That note matters as much as the button. Private staff tools are not shown in this public story.
The site gives a person a calmer place to start. It does not claim to solve every need. It helps them find the next source and question to check.

title: Make the next question easier to ask.
problem: A first-time buyer and a property investor do not arrive with the same question. A single broad sales page cannot explain every next step well.
kept: The personal voice, client-supplied business facts, and direct contact with the lender.
changed: We organized the site by situation. Buyers, homeowners, investors, and realtors have distinct routes into relevant pages and tools.
result: Visitors can find the topic that fits, use public planning tools, and ask a more specific question without starting with one generic form.
body: Logan Loans gives people information about home loans. Some are buying a home. Some want a new loan on a home they own. Others are buying property to rent or sell. We built a site with a clear place for each of those needs.
Warm color, clear type, and local scenes give the site a human feel. The first page helps a person choose a path. It does not ask them to learn a wall of bank terms first.
The next page keeps the detail. A simple opening should not lead to a vague answer. Each path gives the reader more context, with a clear way to ask Logan a question.
The tools page brings loan calculators and guides together. Visitors can explore a monthly payment or the cost of a home. They can look at the numbers before choosing to call.
These tools help with planning. They are not loan offers or approvals. A person still needs a review of their own case. We describe the website here, not the terms of a loan.
Buyer paths link to loan pages, tools, and guides. A contact option stays close as the reader narrows the topic. A visitor need not start with a form before learning the basics.
Business facts and terms have their own pages. The same paths work on a phone. The client controls the loan claims and terms. The case study does not replace that source.
The site helps a visitor learn first and ask next. Its value is a clear path through a hard topic, not a promise that a loan will be approved.

title: The room has a point of view. So does the site.
problem: A venue website must show the feel of the place and answer practical questions. A visitor still needs the menu, location, and a way to check what is on.
kept: The venue’s name, real game-room photographs, supplied menu information, and direct phone and map contacts.
changed: We organized the site around playing, eating, and visiting. Bold type gives it character, while the menu and venue details stay easy to reach.
result: Visitors can explore the room, read the menu, and find directions or a phone number from one public website.
body: The Break Room is a pool hall in Glendale, Arizona. Pool, darts, food, and sports give people reasons to visit. We built a site that brings those choices together. It shows the room’s character and helps a guest plan a night out.
Large type gives the site the feel of a venue poster. The menu breaks the night into clear choices. Each section has its own job, so they do not all compete for the same space.
The page uses real venue photos and labeled concept art. The labels stay with the work. We do not pass off a planned look as a photo of a finished room.

title: A personal service with a clear first step.
problem: Someone new to tarot may not know what to ask or which format to choose. The website needed to explain the service without making the choice feel complex.
kept: Rachel’s personal approach, the focus on a conversation, and the clear boundary that the visitor makes their own choices.
changed: We gave the reading formats clear descriptions and next steps. A first-reading guide and a question path help people who are not ready to choose.
result: A visitor can understand the service, compare a voice note with a live conversation, and choose a next step without knowing tarot terms.
body: The Tarot Hotline offers tarot readings with Rachel Hope. We built a site that explains the service before asking someone to choose. A visitor can meet Rachel, compare the options, and find a way to start. No knowledge of tarot is needed.
A red rotary phone gives the site a clear point of view. Deep green, cream, and pink carry that mood through the pages. The look fits the hotline name. It does not make a visitor guess what to do.
The words have the same job. The site says what happens next, rather than making grand claims. Rachel stays part of the story. The visitor stays in charge of their own choices.
The readings page separates a voice note from a live talk. Each choice says how it works and what comes next. A visitor can compare the options without having to work out a hidden set of plans.
Unsure visitors can ask Rachel a question before paying. A guide for a first reading covers the basics. There is a clear path for people who are not ready to choose.
Each reading leads to the right form, time choice, or Square payment step. The site explains those steps before the handoff. Looking at this case study does not buy a reading.
Questions, terms, and privacy notes have their own pages. The work shown here is the website. It makes no claim to predict events or take the place of expert advice.
The site makes a personal service easier to grasp. It leaves room for curiosity, with the format, cost, and next step clear on the client’s pages.
